steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
Intro
- perching done robustly/accurately by animal fliers: birds, bees, flies, bats
- surfaces arbitrarily oriented or moving unpredictably -> land in unstructured environments to surveil territory, hitchhike on larger animals, pollinate plants, rest
- robots: perching crucial for fully autonomous operation in unstructured environments
- potential: long-term inspections, surveillance, reconnaissance, rapid release/retrieval for missions
- drawback: limited battery life, max flight times tens of minutes -> perching expands operational lifetime of quadrotors
- urban environments: flat surfaces (walls, ceilings) abundant; camera surveillance, sensor reading, radio relay in disaster zones don't need continuous flight

## I-A Dynamic Perching and Challenges
- small aerial robots (quadrotors): agile, load-carrying, but not yet animal-level perching
- dynamic perching (rapid maneuvers, velocity constraints) = one of most significant challenges
- vital on rapidly moving or inverted (ceiling-like) surfaces: accelerate against gravity, rapidly alter orientation
- complex distance-velocity-attitude sensing/control problem under time and motor constraints
- control 3D linear velocity; predict imminent impact; adjust body orientation + landing gear/legs via rapid angular maneuvers
- within milliseconds -> proper body inversion and contact force
- limited onboard computation for sensing, control, planning in small fliers
- accurate sensory estimates under tight timing hard (few ms delay -> crash), esp. unstructured environments
- under-actuated -> hard to do maneuvers needing uncoupled linear + angular acceleration
- acrobatic flight: high thrust, extreme angular accelerations, motor limits, unmodeled behaviors
- need computationally efficient algorithms; physically-embodied intelligence (landing gear/legs) reduces computation, adds robustness
- inverted landing (Figure 1) harder than horizontal/vertical: gravity works against robot
- emulate flies: approach from variety of directions
- stringent, variable constraints on linear velocity (avoid falls, sufficient adhesion) and body orientation (proper contact, avoid collision)

## I-B Inverted Landing in Flies
- flies solved dynamic perching
- sequence of coordinated maneuvers, less than 100 ms
- upward acceleration -> rapid body rotation + leg extension -> leg-assisted body swing pivoting on fore-legs attached to ceiling
- different approach directions -> diverse behaviors (axes of rotation, angular rates)
- success explained by timely triggering + control of rotational maneuvers (flips), correlated with optical flows extracted by visual system
- mechanical + computational intelligence: position legs and tarsi before impact (Figure 1); dissipate impact force, recover from failed landing
- efficient visuomotor mapping: direct connections between visual system and motor neurons -> rapid motor program selection/timing, reactive aerobatic maneuvers
- insect vision evolved for optical flow: encodes translational velocity, distance to surface, time-to-contact; no feature identification/tracking
- optical flow widely used in nature; animals of various sizes follow robust perception-based landing trajectories

## I-C Goal and Contributions
- previous (conference) work: 3D control policy region, effects of landing gear design; initial simulation + limited experiments
- now: general two-stage control policy inspired by flies; mappings from optical-flow cues to triggering + control of rotational maneuvers
- generalizes discrete sensory-motor pairs from reinforcement learning (conference framework), in refined simulation; maps augmented optical-flow space to motor actions
- unlike trajectory planning/tracking methods: diverse behaviors via motor control and touchdown; integrates computational + mechanical intelligence
- sim-to-real transfer to physical quadrotor; domain randomization + system identification; zero-shot
- experiments under variety of approach conditions; range of successful inverted landings
- influence of leg design geometry on success and robustness

## I-D Organization
- Section II: literature on robotic landing (computational + mechanical intelligence)
- Section III: two-stage policy + training
- Section IV: simulation setup + experiments
- Section V: performance, results, landing gear designs
- Section VI: conclusions, future work
- Appendix A: system identification details

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Perching is something animal fliers do all the time, with robustness and accuracy, for example birds, bees, flies, and bats. Because they can perch on surfaces that are arbitrarily oriented or that move unpredictably, animal fliers are able to land in unstructured environments so they can surveil territory, hitchhike on larger animals to travel to new places, pollinate plants, or rest.

Getting similar perching abilities in flying robots is crucial to allow them to operate fully autonomously in unstructured environments, and it could enable or augment long-term inspections, surveillance, reconnaissance, and the rapid release and retrieval of robots for different missions. A big drawback of these robot systems in recent years is their limited battery life, which usually only gives maximum flight times of tens of minutes. Because of this, being able to perch on targeted objects can greatly extend the operational lifetime of quadrotor robots. This could be especially useful in urban environments, where there are lots of flat surfaces like walls and ceilings and where many tasks like camera surveillance, sensor reading, and acting as a radio relay in disaster zones do not need continuous flight.

## I-A Dynamic Perching and Challenges

Small aerial robots like quadrotors show impressive aerial agility and load-carrying capacity, but they still do not have the perching capabilities we see in animal fliers. In fact dynamic perching, which involves rapid maneuvers and is subject to velocity constraints, is still one of the biggest challenges for aerial robots. This skill is vital when landing on surfaces that move fast or are inverted (ceiling-like), since the flier has to accelerate against gravity and change its orientation quickly. In these cases the flier has to solve a complex distance-velocity-attitude sensing and control problem with strict time and motor constraints. The small flier needs to control its 3D linear velocity, predict the coming impact accurately, and adjust its body orientation and landing gear/legs relative to the perching surface in time, using rapid angular maneuvers. These maneuvers have to be done within milliseconds so that the touchdown has proper body inversion and contact force.

The challenges of perching are not only about the maneuver itself, they also involve the limited computational resources that small fliers have for sensing, control, and planning. It is very hard to get accurate onboard sensory estimates within the strict time constraints of dynamic perching (for example a delay of just a few milliseconds could cause a crash), especially in unstructured environments. Aerial robots are also usually under-actuated, which makes it hard to do aggressive maneuvers that need uncoupled linear and angular acceleration. Also, aggressive acrobatic flight needs high thrust and extreme angular accelerations that can push the motors of the robots to their limits, which can lead to unmodeled behaviors. So a successful perching strategy has to take these limitations into account and use computationally efficient algorithms if it is going to replicate the perching behaviors of animal fliers. Importantly, physically-embodied intelligence, like in the landing gear or legs, can help reduce the computational demands and make things more robust.

Inverted landing (Figure 1) is also much harder than landing on horizontal or vertical surfaces, because gravity works against the robot as it gets close to the landing surface. Also, to really emulate the behavior of flies, the robots have to be able to approach the surface from many different directions. This adds strict and variable constraints both on the linear velocity, which is needed to prevent falling down and to make sure there is enough adhesion on contact, and on the body orientation, which has to be controlled accurately to get proper contact and avoid collision.

## I-B Inverted Landing in Flies
- flies solved dynamic perching
- coordinated maneuvers, less than 100 ms: upward acceleration -> rapid body rotation + leg extension -> leg-assisted body swing on fore-legs attached to ceiling
- different approach directions -> diverse behaviors (axes of rotation, angular rates)
- success explained by timely triggering + control of flips, correlated with optical flows
- mechanical + computational intelligence: legs and tarsi positioned before impact (Figure 1); dissipate impact, recover from failed landing
- direct visual system -> motor neuron connections; rapid motor program selection, reactive aerobatic maneuvers
- insect vision evolved for optical flow: translational velocity, distance, time-to-contact, no feature tracking
- optical flow widely used in nature for robust perception-based landing

## I-C Goal and Contributions of the Current Work
- builds on previous conference work (3D control policy region, landing gear design, initial sim + limited experiments)
- general two-stage control policy inspired by flies: optical-flow cues -> triggering + control of rotational maneuvers
- generalizes RL sensory-motor pairs in refined simulation; augmented optical-flow space -> motor actions
- unlike trajectory planning/tracking: diverse behaviors emerge; integrates computational + mechanical intelligence
- zero-shot sim-to-real on physical quadrotor (domain randomization, system identification)
- experiments under variety of approach conditions; leg design geometry vs success and robustness

## I-D Organization of the Paper
- Section II literature; Section III policy + training; Section IV simulation + experiments; Section V results + landing gear; Section VI conclusions; Appendix A system identification

## I-A Dynamic Perching and Challenges

These maneuvers have to be done within milliseconds so that the touchdown has proper body inversion and contact force.

It is very hard to get accurate onboard sensory estimates within the strict time constraints of dynamic perching (for example a delay of just a few milliseconds could cause a crash), especially in unstructured environments. Aerial robots are also usually under-actuated, which makes it hard to do aggressive maneuvers that need uncoupled linear and angular acceleration. Also, aggressive acrobatic flight needs high thrust and extreme angular accelerations that can push the motors of the robots to their limits, which can lead to unmodeled behaviors. So a successful perching strategy has to take these limitations into account and use computationally efficient algorithms if it is going to replicate the perching behaviors of animal fliers. Importantly, physically-embodied intelligence, like in the landing gear or legs, can help reduce the computational demands and make things more robust.

Inverted landing (Figure 1) is also much harder than landing on horizontal or vertical surfaces, because gravity works against the robot as it gets close to the landing surface. Also, to really emulate the behavior of flies, the robots have to be able to approach the surface from many different directions. This adds strict and variable constraints both on the linear velocity, which is needed to prevent falling down and to make sure there is enough adhesion on contact, and on the body orientation, which has to be controlled accurately to get proper contact and avoid collision.

## I-B Inverted Landing in Flies

Flies, for example, have solved the dynamic perching problem. Their solution is a sequence of well-coordinated maneuvers that are completed in less than 100 ms and that make an inverted landing possible. To start, they accelerate upward, then they rapidly rotate their body and extend their legs, and at the end the flies do a leg-assisted body swing, with their fore-legs (now firmly attached to the ceiling) as a pivot point. It has also been shown that different directions of approaching the ceiling lead to different landing behaviors in terms of the axes of rotation and the angular rates of the body maneuvers. More importantly, the success of these landings can be explained by the timely triggering and proper control of the body rotational maneuvers (or flips), which are both strongly correlated to a number of optical flows that the visual system of flies can extract.

The landing process in flies uses a combination of mechanical and computational intelligence, since they rapidly and precisely position their legs and tarsi before impact (Figure 1), and these are then used to dissipate the impact force or even to recover from a failed landing. Flies are known for their efficient visuomotor mapping and they have direct connections between their visual system and motor neurons. These connections allow rapid motor program selection and timing, so they can do reactive aerobatic maneuvers. In particular, the insect visual system has evolved to extract optical flow efficiently, and optical flow encodes translational velocity, distance to a surface, and time-to-contact without needing hard feature identification and tracking. Visual cues like optical flow are used widely in nature and give animals of different sizes a computationally efficient and effective way to follow robust perception-based landing trajectories.

## I-C Goal and Contributions of the Current Work

This journal submission builds on our previous work, which mainly focused on identifying a capable three-dimensional control policy region and looking at the effects of landing gear design on landing success with initial simulation and limited experimental testing, and it advances our research significantly. In the current study we introduce a general two-stage control policy that is inspired by the inverted landing strategy of flies and that is centered on the mappings from optical flow-based cues to the triggering and control of rotational maneuvers. This control policy generalizes the discrete sensory-motor pairs that we got using reinforcement learning, using the framework shown in our conference proceedings, inside our further refined simulation, and it efficiently maps an augmented optical-flow space to motor control actions. Our strategy is different from existing methods that rely on trajectory planning and tracking, because it lets diverse behaviors emerge through motor control and touchdown processes, so computational and mechanical intelligence can be closely integrated.

To validate the approach, we transferred the generalized inverted-landing policy from simulation to real-world experiments with a physical quadrotor, and we used domain randomization and system identification techniques for zero-shot transfer. Then, with a series of experiments under many different approach conditions, we showed a range of successful inverted landings. We also looked at how the geometry of the leg design influences the overall success and robustness of the inverted landing.

## I-D Organization of the Paper

In Section II we go through the literature on robotic landing, looking at both computational and mechanical intelligence-based methods. Section III presents the proposed two-stage general control policy for inverted landing and how it is trained in detail. Section IV describes our simulation setup and the experimental testing process. Section V discusses the performance of our work, the results we got, and the possible benefits of different landing gear designs. The last section, Section VI, gives the conclusions of the study and suggests directions for future research. More details on system identifications and relevant explanations are in Appendix A.

steps.text:
Perching is a feat routinely performed by animal fliers with robustness and accuracy, as seen in birds [1,2,3], bees [4,5,6,7,8,9], flies [10,11,12], and bats [13,14]. With the ability to perch on surfaces that are arbitrarily oriented or moving unpredictably, animal fliers can land in unstructured environments to surveil territory, hitchhike on larger animals to travel to new locations, pollinate plants, or rest.

Achieving similar perching abilities in flying robots is crucial for enabling their fully autonomous operation in unstructured environments [15], and could enable or augment long-term inspections, surveillance, reconnaissance, and the rapid release and retrieval of robots for various missions [16,17,18,19,20]. A major drawback of these robot systems in recent years has been their limited battery life, which typically only sustains maximum flight times on the scale of tens of minutes [21]. For this reason, the ability to perch on targeted objects can greatly expand the operational lifetime of quadrotor robots. This capability could be particularly useful in urban environments, where flat surfaces like walls and ceilings are abundant and many tasks, such as camera surveillance, sensor reading, and acting as a radio relay in disaster zones, do not require continuous flight [22,17,16].

## I-A Dynamic Perching and Challenges

Despite the impressive aerial agility and load-carrying capacity of small aerial robots like quadrotors, they have yet to achieve the perching capabilities of animal fliers. Indeed, dynamic perching, which is characterized by rapid maneuvers and subject to velocity constraints, still poses one of the most significant challenges for aerial robots. This skill becomes vital when landing on rapidly moving or inverted (ceiling-like) surfaces, requiring the flier to accelerate against gravity and rapidly alter its orientation. In such scenarios, fliers must solve a complex distance-velocity-attitude sensing and control problem under stringent time and motor constraints. The small flier must control its 3D linear velocity [23,5], accurately predict imminent impact [24,25], and adjust in time its body orientation and landing gear/legs relative to the perching surface through rapid angular maneuvers. These maneuvers must be executed within milliseconds to ensure a touchdown with proper body inversion and contact force [10].

The challenges of perching extend beyond the maneuver itself and involve the limited computational resources available for sensing, control, and planning in small fliers [25,26]. Achieving accurate onboard sensory estimations within the stringent time constraints of dynamic perching is a formidable task (e.g., a delay of only a few milliseconds could result in a crash), especially in unstructured environments. Aerial robots are also commonly under-actuated, which makes it difficult to execute aggressive maneuvers that demand uncoupled linear and angular acceleration. Moreover, aggressive acrobatic flight requires high thrust and extreme angular accelerations that can push the robots' motors to their limits, potentially leading to unmodeled behaviors. A successful perching strategy must therefore consider these limitations and rely on computationally efficient algorithms to replicate the perching behaviors of animal fliers. Importantly, physically-embodied intelligence [27,28], as seen in landing gear or legs, can help mitigate computational demands and improve robustness.

Inverted landing (Figure 1) also presents a much greater challenge than landing on horizontal or vertical surfaces, because gravity works against the robot as it approaches the landing surface. Furthermore, to truly emulate the behavior of flies, robots must be able to approach the surface from a variety of directions [10]. This introduces stringent and variable constraints both on the linear velocity, which is essential to prevent downward falls and ensure sufficient adhesion upon contact, and on the body orientation, which must be accurately controlled to ensure proper contact and avoid collision.

## I-B Inverted Landing in Flies

Flies, for example, have successfully solved the dynamic perching problem [29]. Their solution is a sequence of well-coordinated maneuvers, completed in less than 100 ms, that make an inverted landing possible [10]. They begin with an upward acceleration, followed by a rapid rotation of the body and an extension of the legs; the sequence ends with a leg-assisted body swing, using the fore-legs, now firmly attached to the ceiling, as a pivot point. Moreover, it has been shown that different ceiling-approach directions lead to diverse landing behaviors in terms of axes of rotation and angular rates of body maneuvers [10]. More importantly, the success of these landings can be explained by the timely triggering and proper control of body rotational maneuvers (or flips), both of which are strongly correlated to a number of optical flows that the flies' visual system can extract.

The landing process in flies combines mechanical and computational intelligence, as they rapidly and precisely position their legs and tarsi prior to impact (Figure 1) and then use them to dissipate impact force or even recover from a failed landing. Known for their efficient visuomotor mapping, flies have direct connections between their visual system and motor neurons. These connections enable rapid motor program selection and timing, and thus reactive aerobatic maneuvers [15]. In particular, the insect visual system has evolved for efficient extraction of optical flow [30], which encodes translational velocity, distance to a surface, and time-to-contact without the need for arduous feature identification and tracking. Visual cues like optical flow are widely used in nature and provide a computationally efficient and effective way for animals of various sizes to follow robust perception-based landing trajectories [4,1].

## I-C Goal and Contributions of the Current Work

Building upon our previous work [25], which focused primarily on identifying a capable three-dimensional control policy region and exploring the effects of landing gear design on landing success through initial simulation and limited experimental testing, this journal submission significantly advances our research. The current study introduces a general two-stage control policy, inspired by the inverted landing strategy of flies, that centers on the mappings from optical flow-based cues to the triggering and control of rotational maneuvers. This control policy generalizes the discrete sensory-motor pairs obtained using reinforcement learning, with the framework shown in our conference proceedings, inside our further refined simulation, and efficiently maps an augmented optical-flow space to motor control actions. Unlike existing methods that rely on trajectory planning and tracking, our strategy promotes the emergence of diverse behaviors via motor control and touchdown processes, enabling the close integration of computational and mechanical intelligence.

To validate our approach, we transferred the generalized inverted-landing policy from simulation to real-world experiments with a physical quadrotor, using domain randomization and system identification techniques for zero-shot transfer. Through a series of experiments under a variety of approach conditions, we then demonstrated a range of successful inverted landings. We also investigated the influence of leg design geometry on the overall success and robustness of the inverted landing.

## I-D Organization of the Paper

In Section II, we review the literature on robotic landing, covering both computational and mechanical intelligence-based methods. Section III presents in detail the proposed two-stage general control policy for inverted landing and its training methodology. Section IV describes our simulation setup and the experimental testing process. In Section V, we discuss the performance of our work, the results achieved, and the potential benefits of varying landing gear designs. Finally, Section VI draws conclusions from our study and suggests avenues for future research. Additional details on system identifications and relevant explanations are provided in Appendix A.
